purpose: Briefs whose deciding fact exists only in the user's head. The screen asks one question: does this class of brief open the commit-versus-ask channel? It is not a wording experiment and makes no claim about the 27.5-point polarity result.
provenance: Authored 2026-11-20, after the second brief screen (modes-experiment-log.md §29) failed to find an ownership-ambiguous brief of a different class. The idea is ECC's hidden-intent harness (docs/gateguard/question-effectiveness.md:206), which exists because a deciding fact held only by a simulated user produces a genuine ask.

briefs.brief: The nightly job failed again. Sort it out.
briefs.hiddenIntent: Whether the user wants service restored tonight (incident) or the cause removed (debug), and whether the job may be disabled meanwhile.

briefs.brief: We need to change how customers are billed next quarter.
briefs.hiddenIntent: Whether this is a price change, an invoicing change, or a tax change.
Which number is wrong, and what the correct value should be.

briefs.brief: Make the API faster before launch.
briefs.hiddenIntent: The latency target and the load it must hold.

briefs.brief: Clean up the repo before the audit.
briefs.hiddenIntent: Whether the audit is security, licence or process.

briefs.brief: The docs are out of date.
briefs.hiddenIntent: Which document, and which reader it must serve.
Whether the user wants a suite strategy or faster individual tests.
Whether the missing thing is a plan, a schema change, or an owner.
What the review is for: correctness, risk, security, or a go/no-go decision.
Whether the cost is cloud spend or model tokens, and what trade is acceptable.

control.brief: Explain why this module is structured the way it is.
control.why: The one brief of seven that passed the screen (modes-experiment-log.md §28). Interleaved with the hidden-intent briefs so the ask rate has a within-run comparator rather than a remembered number.
